analysis.title: Global Views: Downside Growth Risks
key_insights: Global growth in 2026 has been in line with potential GDP for both the world and the G3. GS reads this as fiscal easing and the AI boom offsetting the drag from the war in Iran and higher US tariffs.
GS standing forecasts project more of the same growth in 2027, as lower energy prices offset fading fiscal and AI tailwinds. The balance of risks is to the downside.

Energy prices have climbed again on fears of renewed Middle East escalation. Gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and European/Asian natural gas are near or above their March/April highs, which is likely to hurt consumers and energy-importing economies.

Longer-term yields have risen about 100bp on average across DM yield curves since early 2026, driven by large deficits, AI-linked borrowing and central bank hikes. If sustained, GS estimates a cumulative 0.6% drag on GDP via housing, consumer durables and business investment.
Only part of the yield drag is in GS forecasts, because GS expects yields to pull back as central banks deliver fewer hikes than the market prices.

The AI growth impulse was set to peak in late 2026 or early 2027 even before concerns about the sustainability of AI investment intensified in recent weeks. GS expects AI investment as a share of GDP to rise more slowly over the next year, which will weigh on capex growth, especially in the US.

AI-driven stock gains added an estimated 0.4pp (0.25% of GDP) to US consumer spending growth over the past year. The effect should fade gradually if stocks track GS strategists' expectations, and faster if AI-related stocks keep falling.

GS's base case is that AI investment will pay off in higher productivity and profits, but labor market disruption is a key channel and has negative near-term effects. Across US nonmanufacturing industries, AI adoption correlates significantly negatively with employment growth and positively with unemployment.

The Fed's signals (explicit from Williams and Jefferson, implicit from Warsh) effectively rule out a hike on October 28. GS still sees a 25bp hike to 4-4.25% on December 9 as very likely because spot inflation remains too high.

GS expects significant disinflation in 2027 as tariff, energy and AI-price impulses fade, but risks are to the upside, most obviously in energy. Higher inflation could bring another hike in March. Either way GS sees renewed cuts in late 2027 or early 2028.

The ECB will likely hold next week and deliver a final hike to 2.75% in December. French bond market turbulence poses greater downside risk to that call than in the US. It has tightened financial conditions enough to cut 1/4 to 1/2pp from annualized growth in coming quarters.

If the French turbulence intensifies into December, markets might read an ECB hike as insufficient focus on Euro area fragmentation. The ECB could pair a hike with renewed balance sheet expansion, but the hurdle is high because buying French bonds raises moral hazard concerns.

GS expects the Bank of England to raise Bank Rate by 25bp to 4% on November 5. UK GDP has surprised to the upside this year and unemployment fell to 4.7% in August on a 3-month average. Rising inflation and a January household energy price reset risk further hikes, but market pricing of 4+ hikes (including November) looks excessive.
GS also expects hikes in Canada and New Zealand this week and in Australia next week.

GS raised its 2026 China GDP forecast to 4.6% after slightly faster Q3 growth, but most activity indicators are weaker. Property activity and fixed asset investment are contracting y/y, and large retailers still post substantial y/y sales declines.

Sustaining GDP growth in China's official 4.5-5% target range requires continued steep increases in the trade surplus, which is already 1% of global GDP. Trading partners may respond with trade barriers, although measures so far have been limited.

GS's strongest global view is that central banks will deliver fewer hikes than priced. GS rates strategists see underweight positioning and diminished technical risks as reasons the recent rally may extend.
GS equity strategists are wary of momentum factor exposure given narrow breadth, but expect the S&P 500 to resume its climb after the midterm election on solid earnings growth.
GS credit strategists stay cautious on IG technology bonds but see scope for a near-term reversal in HY after the recent selloff.
GS FX strategists expect the yen to hedge further AI jitters, partly because such jitters would narrow US-Japan rate differentials.
GS commodity strategists recommend targeted exposure to oil products and European natural gas to hedge near-term escalation risks, plus longer-term exposure to copper, gold and select power markets.

risk_factors: Renewed Middle East escalation pushing energy prices higher and hurting consumers and energy importers.
Sustained 100bp rise in DM long-term yields, a cumulative 0.6% GDP drag.
Fading AI investment impulse and a sharper decline in the AI wealth effect if AI stocks keep falling.
AI-related labor market disruption spreading beyond the technology sector.
Higher inflation, particularly from energy, which could bring another Fed hike in March.
French bond market turbulence tightening Euro area financial conditions and cutting 1/4 to 1/2pp from annualized growth.
China's rising trade surplus provoking trade barriers abroad.
Contracting Chinese property and fixed asset investment alongside weak domestic demand.
charts_described: Exhibit 3 shows the cumulative GDP effect of a 100bp rate increase across the curve by country, split into housing, consumers/credit/cashflow, corporates/capex and debt/deficits channels.
Exhibit 4 shows estimated AI wealth effects on annualized QoQ real PCE growth under upside (AI stocks +55%, other +20%), baseline and downside (AI stocks -40%, other -15%) scenarios.
Exhibit 5 shows regressions of employment growth = -0.3 - 0.09 * AI adoption (t-stat -2.07) and unemployment rate = -2 + 0.09 * AI adoption (t-stat 4.20).
Exhibit 6 shows Fed funds scenario analysis with probabilities of 35% (three hikes), 50% (two hikes then cuts to 3.25-3.5%, GS baseline) and 15% (recession).

tension_points.bull_case: GS expects fewer hikes than priced by markets: the Fed delivers one more hike in December and the ECB a final hike in December, so bonds can rally from underweight positioning.
tension_points.bear_case: Higher energy-driven inflation could bring another Fed hike in March, and GS gives 35% to three hikes with a higher terminal rate.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Energy prices staying near or above March/April highs and pushing inflation higher, which could mean another Fed hike in March.

tension_points.bull_case: GS base case is that AI investment pays off in higher productivity and economywide profits, and strategists expect the S&P 500 to resume its climb after the midterms.
tension_points.bear_case: The growth impulse peaks in late 2026 or early 2027, the wealth effect fades, and AI adoption is linked to weaker employment and higher unemployment beyond tech.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI-related stocks continuing to decline, which would fade the consumer wealth effect more sharply.
